title: Teaching and Learning Across Cultures: A Language Educator's Perspective

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about what language teaching looks like when you take seriously the global and intercultural dimensions of language use. For a long time — and in many classrooms still today — language teaching was premised on an idealised native speaker model. The goal was to get learners to approximate, as closely as possible, the language of an educated British or American speaker. In terms of what we now know about how language works globally, this model is seriously outdated.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: Consider what it actually means to communicate successfully in English internationally. The most common situation is not a non-native speaker interacting with a native speaker, but two or more non-native speakers from different first-language backgrounds interacting with each other. In this situation, the relevant norms are not British or American English — they are the norms of ELF: clarity, effective repair strategies, accommodation to the interlocutor, and flexibility.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: From the perspective of language teaching, this suggests a significant reorientation. Rather than teaching learners to aim for native-speaker accuracy, we should be teaching communicative effectiveness. Rather than treating non-standard features of learner English as errors to be corrected, we should ask: does this feature impede communication? If not, it may be an acceptable feature of a learner's emerging variety, not a mistake to be stamped out.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: This does not mean abandoning standards or accepting anything. There are features of language use that do impede communication — that cause confusion, misunderstanding, or ambiguity — and these are the appropriate targets of instruction. In the interests of the learner's communicative success, teachers need to prioritise what actually matters for intelligibility. With a view to helping learners function effectively in international contexts, the curriculum needs to reflect the realities of global English use, not the assumptions of a monocultural classroom.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: Intercultural competence is, in this framework, not a supplement to language learning but an integral part of it. Understanding that different cultures have different communication norms — different expectations about directness, silence, eye contact, turn-taking, and disagreement — is as important as understanding grammar. A learner who can construct grammatically perfect sentences but misreads the communicative intent of their interlocutor has not succeeded in communication.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: By virtue of their position, language teachers have an opportunity and a responsibility to develop intercultural citizens — people who can navigate the world's linguistic and cultural diversity with competence, curiosity, and respect. This is not just about teaching language; it is about forming the communicative identities of people who will work, learn, and live in an increasingly interconnected world. The classroom is a microcosm of that world, and what happens in it matters.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Pemberton
dialogue.text: Let me close with a provocation. The question "how good is your English?" is deeply ambiguous. Good for what? Good by whose standards? Good in which context? A Brazilian engineer collaborating with a Korean team on a project managed through English might have perfectly adequate English for this purpose without being able to pass a Cambridge Advanced exam. Conversely, a learner who achieves a very high exam score may still struggle with the messy, fast, and culturally loaded reality of international communication. In the interests of genuine communicative competence, we need to ask better questions than "how good is your English?"
